lesson_title: Weigh the Whole Train First: Connected Bodies and Pulleys
hook_text: A 5 kg mass hangs from a string. The string carries 22 newtons — not 49. And that is not a mistake.
clip_script: A mass hangs over a pulley, dragging a block across a bench. The mass weighs 49 newtons. The string carries 22. Everyone says that is impossible — the string must hold the whole weight! Watch. If the string DID pull with the full 49, the forces on the mass would balance, and a balanced mass does not fall. It just hangs. But this mass is accelerating downward, so the weight has to WIN against the tension. Tension below the hanging weight is not an error — it is the signature of acceleration. Now the method, two moves. Move one: weigh the whole train. Add the masses, count only outside forces — the string's tugs cancel inside. Forty-nine driving, minus five comma nine of friction, over eight kilograms: five comma four metres per second squared. Move two: zoom in on the laziest object, the dangler. Forty-nine minus T equals five times five comma four — T is 22. Whole train first, one wagon second. Every pulley question ever, in two moves.
visual_style: A bench-edge pulley setup with the string glowing and a live tension readout; a tug-of-war meter between 49 and 22; then the two-move recipe stamped over the diagram as the system slides.
mood: Confident myth-busting — a wrong intuition dismantled in real time.
pacing: Bold claim up front, slow-motion balance argument, brisk two-move recipe to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never fear a pulley question again.
